textClass.keywords: Spatial probit Multivariate normal probabilities Spatial auto-regressive model Spatial error model Spatial discrete choice models

div.p: A new estimation method for spatial binary probit models is presented. Both spatial auto-regressive (SAR) and spatial error (SEM) models are considered. The proposed estimator relies on the approximation of the likelihood function, that follows a multivariate normal distribution which parameters depend on the spatial structure of the observations. The approximation is inspired by the univariate conditioning procedure proposed by Mendell and Elston, with some modifications to improve accuracy and speed. Very accurate parameter estimations have been achieved in reasonable time for simulated data samples with as much as one million observations. The lessons learned in the Monte Carlo experiment have been applied to a case study on urban sprawl over more than forty thousands plots in Southern France.

div.head: Introduction
div.p: Spatial binary choice models belong to the family of econometrics methods that deals with observations showing some kind of spatial or network dependence. Particularly, spatial binary choice models deals with observations where the dependent variable can only take two separate values, such as the choice of adopting a new farming technology (Case, 1992), increasing tax rates in a district (Beron and Vijverberg, 2004), reopening of a damaged infrastructure (LeSage et al., 2011), the choice of location of suppliers plants (Klier and McMillen, 2008), of R & D labs (Autant-Bernard, 2006), tree harvesting choice (Fortin et al., 2013), defoliation (Heagerty and Lele, 1998), deforestation (Brun et al., 2015), plants distribution (Collingham et al., 2000) or land use allocation (Carrión-Flores and Irwin, 2004;McMillen and Soppelsa, 2015;Munroe et al., 2004;Wang et al., 2011;Zhong et al., 2011). The ever-increasing availability of large data sets with observable spatial discrete choices raises the question whether existing estimation methods are ready to tackle the challenge of the curse of dimensionality. In fact, contrary to the case of continuous dependent variables with spatial dependence, for which the scientific community has produced an abundant literature, the case of spatial discrete choice models, either binary or multinomial, has received limited attention, mainly due to its complexity (Pinkse and Slade, 2010). In this contribution we will treat only the case of spatial binary choice models, that have been recently reviewed in a work of Calabrese and Elkink (2014). There, the authors compare through a Monte-Carlo experiment all significant contributions in the field: the expectation-maximization (EM) algorithm by McMillen (1992), the Bayesian Gibbs sampler by LeSage (2000), the recursive importance sampling (RIS) algorithm by Beron and Vijverberg (2004), the generalized method of moments (GMM) by Pinkse and Slade (1998) and its linearised (linearised GMM) version by Klier and McMillen (2008). Also, on the same subject, the unpublished paper of Pace and LeSage (2011) that uses Geweke-Hajivassiliou-Keene (GHK) approximations of a multivariate normal probability with sparse variance-covariance matrix (GHK and RIS are basically the same). From this review, we observed that only RIS and Gibbs sampler estimators perform reasonably well in terms of accuracy, but they are unfeasible for large samples (n ≫ 1000), while, on the other hand, GMM-type estimators scale well w.r.t. sample size, but their accuracy is really poor, especially when the value of the spatial dependence parameter is high. There is hence a need of new estimation techniques that are capable of handling big sample sizes and that at the same time are reasonably accurate in terms of the parameter estimation.

For spatial binary models, the two most used specifications are spatial logit (Klier and McMillen, 2008) and spatial probit (Beron and Vijverberg, 2004;LeSage, 2000;McMillen, 1992;Pace and LeSage, 2011;Pinkse and Slade, 1998;Wang et al., 2013). In contrast with the logit specification, that assumes multivariate logistic distribution of the error terms, the probit model, that assumes multivariate normal (MVN) distribution, is particularly attractive for the flexibility of the MVN covariance structure. We hence propose an estimation technique for spatial probit based on the maximisation of the corresponding likelihood function, a prodigious task according to Wang and Kockelman (2009). In fact, there exists no closed form expression for computing MVN probabilities, that are eventually expressed as a multiple integral and hence no exact way of computing the likelihood function of the corresponding spatial probit model. Therefore, we are forced to resort to an approximation technique that is inspired by the univariate conditioning approximation method proposed by Mendell and Elston (1974), described by Kamakura (1989) and recently reviewed by Connors et al. (2014). We will show in Section 3 that this method allows to compute the log-likelihood of a spatial probit model accurately and rapidly, especially if compared with existing alternatives found in the literature. In Section 3.2, we present two estimation techniques for spatial probit models: one based on full-likelihood maximisation and the other that uses conditional likelihoods. In Section 4 we will then compare the two techniques on a set of simulated Monte Carlo experiments and finally, in Section 5, we will test the performance of the proposed methods on an empirical study on urban sprawl on more than forty thousands parcels of 26 municipalities in Southern France.

div.head: Spatial binary choice models
div.p: Spatial binary-choice regression models are used to analyse sample data that are associated with specific locations in space and that represent binary outcomes (usually actions or choices). We deal with spatial regression models of the following form (the notations follow LeSage and Pace (2008)): y y Xβ u u u ϵ ϵ ρW λM σ I 0 = + + , = + , ∼ ( , ), n 2

where y represents an n × 1 vector of binary dependent variables, X an n k × matrix of independent variables, I n is the identity matrix of size n and β (k × 1 vector), ρ and λ (both scalar in [ -1, 1]) are parameters to be estimated. The two n×n matrices W and M are known as spatial weight matrices and contain the information on the spatial relationship between observations. Spatial weight matrices are usually constructed as a function of the distance between observations or other contiguity measures (shared borders, shared department, etc.). Typically w = 1 ij (or m = 1 ij ), if observations i and j are contiguous, while w = 0 ij (or m = 0 ij ) otherwise (it follows immediately that both W and M are symmetric and by convention, the diagonal is set to zero). It is common practice to row-standardize the spatial weight matrices, i.e. w w w = /(∑ ) ij ij j ij . The model in Eq. ( 1) is often referred as spatial autoregressive model with spatial autoregressive disturbances (or SARAR(1, 1)), when both the parameters ρ, a.k.a. spatial lag parameter, and λ, a.k.a. spatial error parameter, are different from zero. If λ = 0, then we will speak of a spatial autoregressive (SAR, or SARAR(1, 0)) model, while if ρ = 0, we will speak of a spatial error model (SEM, or SARAR(0, 1)). The SAR and SEM models are used to explain spatial dependences of different nature. 1 In this work we will focus in particular on spatial autoregressive and spatial error models. In particular, since the disturbances ϵ in Eq. ( 1) follow a multivariate normal distribution, then we are in the case of a SAR probit or SEM probit specification.

For dealing with this problem, there exists several proposals in the literature, that can be grouped into three main families: numerical integration methods, (see, amongst others, Deák, 1980;Drezner and Wesolowsky, 1990;Drezner, 1994;Fayed and Atiya, 2014;Genz, 1992;Genz andBretz, 1999, 2002;Genz, 2004;Harris and Soms, 1980), simulation methods (see Geweke, 1991;Hajivassiliou and McFadden, 1990;Keane, 1994;Manski and Lerman, 1981) and analytical approximation methods (see Clark, 1961;Cox and Wermuth, 1991;Hohenbichler and Rackwitz, 1983;Joe, 1995;Langdon, 1984Langdon, , 1984;;Mendell and Elston, 1974;Olson and Weissfeld, 1991;Solow, 1990;Tang and Melchers, 1986). Our proposal belongs to the last category and is presented in the next section.

div.p: Variable reordering for improved accuracy. The iterations of the Mendell and Elston algorithm follow the order of the observations as given by the problem, but there exists evidence that different reorderings can lead to better approximations (Connors et al., 2014;Gibson et al., 1994;Schervish, 1984). If there were an exact solution to the integral, these orderings would not change the value of the probability, as long as integration limits and rows and columns of Σ are rearranged accordingly, but since we are using an approximation that runs iteratively over the n observations, it is advisable to control the propagation of the approximation error. For that, Gibson et al. (1994) proposed to sort the observations in such a way that the outermost integrals correspond to those observations that have the smallest expected values (a recent study by Connors et al. (2014) corroborates this hypothesis). Since the integral limits are recomputed at each iteration of the algorithm, then also the reordering has to be rerun iteratively. One drawback of this procedure is that it requires the stepwise construction of the Cholesky factor of Σ and it quickly becomes unfeasible, as the sample size increases. We hence implemented a reduced version that uses a unique reordering of the observations before the computation of the likelihood. A comparison of the two reordering schemes is proposed in the Monte Carlo experiment of Section 4.1.

div.head: Numerical considerations for application to large samples
div.p: The numerical approximation presented in the preceding paragraph can be directly used to compute the likelihood associated to SAR and SEM probit models through Eqs. (4) and (7). Nevertheless, there are a few further precautions that we adopted in order to reduce the computation time of the algorithm and improve the quality of the approximation:

• use of sparse matrices and sparse linear algebra, especially for the computations relative to the spatial weight matrices W and M, that have dimension n×n, but usually high sparsity (lot of zero entries);
• the inverse matrices

• the most time-consuming part of the entire algorithm is the Cholesky decomposition of the sparse matrix Σ (n×n). The length of this part depends strongly on the number of non-zero elements of Σ, that in turns depends on the sparsity of W and on the order of the Taylor approximation o W of I ρW ( -) n -1 or I λM ( -) n -1 detailed in the previous point. There exists several algorithms that allow to reduce the number of non-zero elements in the Cholesky factor, based on a clever reordering of the rows and columns of Σ (a.k.a. pivoting). We chosen to perform the Approximate Minimum Degree algorithm (AMD, see Amestoy et al., 1996) before the Cholesky decomposition, since it proved to be really fast and efficient: it slightly worsens the accuracy of the MVN probability, but busts the computation time by several order of magnitude.
The complete algorithm for the computation of the likelihood function can be found in Appendix A.

div.head: Likelihood function and optimization techniques
div.p: For the estimation of the parameters β ρ ( , ) or β λ ( , ) , we propose two optimisation procedures: FL Maximisation of the full log-likelihood by means of a multidimensional optimisation algorithm (it uses the gradient functions reported in Appendix B); CL Maximisation of the log-likelihood conditional to ρ (resp. λ): at each iteration of the optimisation algorithm, a value ρ is used to compute X I ρW X * = ( -) n -1

and then the β para- meters are estimated by means of a Standard Probit regression of y over X * . In this way, the log-likelihood is computed as a function of just ρ and the one-dimensional optimisation algorithm tries to find the ρ that minimize its value.foot_0 Furthermore, one may consider the use of the precision matrix P Σ = -1 instead of the variance-covariance matrix Σ, as suggested by Pace and Barry (1997) and LeSage and Pace (2008). This proposal makes perfectly sense, since P is usually sparser than Σ, and allows a faster Cholesky decomposition. Obviously, the accuracy of the approximation is reduced. Further details on the implementation of the precision-matrix version can be found in Pace and LeSage (2011). In Section 4 we will compare the performances of the approximation method with the full variance-covariance matrix and the one with the precision matrix.

To summarise, our proposal consists of four estimators for the SAR and SEM probit model: FLUC Full log-likelihood with univariate conditional approximation of MVN probabilities and variance-covariance matrix; CLUC Conditional log-likelihood with the univariate conditional approximation of MVN probabilities and variance-covariance matrix; FLUP Full log-likelihood with univariate conditional approximation of MVN probabilities and precision matrix; CLUP Conditional log-likelihood with univariate conditional approximation of MVN probabilities and precision matrix;

In theory, full-likelihood approaches (FLUC and FLUP) are expected to be more accurate, but slower, than the corresponding conditional methods (CLUC and CLUP). Similarly, the versions with the variance-covariance matrix (FLUC and CLUC) are expected to be more accurate, but slower, than the one with precision matrix (FLUP and CLUP), especially when the size n and/or the density of non-zero elements of W increase.

div.head: Monte Carlo simulations
div.p: We planned three Monte Carlo experiments:

1. the first experiment compares the performance of the RIS estimator of Beron and Vijverberg (2004) and three CLUC methods with different reordering schemes. 2. the second experiment is intended to compare the full-likelihood method vs. the condition method; 3. the third experiment tests the performance of the conditional method in terms of accuracy and estimation time for increasing sample sizes.
In all the three experiments, the simulated data are generated using the DGPs detailed in Eq. ( 2) for the SAR probit and in Eq. ( 5) for the SEM probit. The parameters that can vary are:

• the sample size n, • the number of neighbours nn and • the true value ρ for SAR (resp. λ for SEM) of the spatial parameter, while the covariates X 1 ∼ ( , ( -1, 1)), the true parameters β = (0, 1) and the disturbances I 0 ϵ ∼ ( , ) n . 3 In light of the results of the experiments on the order of the Taylor approximation of I ρW ( -

For each observation, the number nn determines the set of its closest neighbours w.r.t. Euclidean distance. These settings are inspired to the choices made in the Monte Carlo simulations of Calabrese and Elkink (2014), with only minor changes (there X 1 ∼ ( , (2, 4)), β = (4, -2) and W has a fixed number of neighbors nn).

The simulations were performed on a Linux High Performance Computing cluster platform (INRA MIGALE bioinformatics platform http://migale.jouy.inra.fr) composed by 580 CPUs of various generations (Intel or AMD processors, quad, six and ten cores from 2.2 to 2.8 Ghz) on 60 computing nodes. The algorithms for the likelihood functions and the corresponding gradients of the second and third experiment have been written in C++ code and embedded in R by means of the Rcpp (Eddelbuettel and François, 2011;Eddelbuettel, 2013) and RcppEigen (Bates and Eddelbuettel, 2013) libraries, an include all the numerical considerations of Section 3.1. For the first experiment, in sake of a fair comparison against the RIS estimator of Beron and Vijverberg (2004) (coded in Rfoot_2 ), the algorithm have been written in simple R code, without the numerical precautions detailed in Section 3.1 (no sparse algebra, Taylor approximation of I ρW ( -) n -1 or pivoting for the Cholesky factorization).

div.head: Experiment 1: Reordering scheme and a comparison with existing algorithms
div.p: In this experiment we intended to test the performance on a SAR probit model of the RIS estimator against our proposal, with the following three reordering schemes:
• No reordering: the observations are not reordered;
• One reordering: the observations are reordered only once, according to the permutation
is in increasing order.
• Complete reordering: observations are reordered iteratively at each step of the algorithm (for the details, see Gibson et al. (1994) or Section 2.2 of Trinh and Genz (2015)).

We chosen the RIS estimator for two main reasons: first of all, because it is also a method based on maximum approximate likelihood optimization (it uses GHK approximation instead of Mendel-Elston), like our proposals, and secondly, because it proved to outperform other estimators in the recent literature review of Calabrese and Elkink (2014) in terms of accuracy.

The Monte Carlo settings are the following: 1000 repetitions and the DGP generated with n ∈ {500, 1000}, nn=4 and ρ = 0.5. The results of the experiment are presented in Table 1 and Fig. 1. The first conclusion is that the RIS estimator is underperforming w.r.t. our proposals, in terms of both accuracy and efficiency. Even in the worst case, our estimators have a bias of less than 5% of the true value, while the RIS estimator is close to 10%. This is specially true for the spatial dependence parameter ρ. In terms of execution time, an average RIS estimation takes at least twice the time than our more time-consuming algorithm (and no less than 30 times our fastest). Furthermore, the computation time of RIS method is strongly affected by the random sampling used in the algorithm, as we can observe in the right panel of Fig. 1.

Regarding the effects of the reordering schemes, we observe that the complete reordering (denoted all in Table 1 and Fig. 1) has the best performance in terms of accuracy, but it is very time consuming w.r.t. other reordering schemes: 17 times the execution time of the algorithm without reordering and 9 times the algorithm with one reordering. The computations with one reordering gives better results than the case without reordering (the bias is comparable in mean, but it has lower variance and its distribution is more pointed), with a moderate increase in computation time. It seems then that the most reasonable choice is to use one reordering, since it is good compromise between accuracy and estimation time. In light of these results, we will adopt the unique reordering scheme throughout the rest of the paper.

div.head: Experiment 2: Conditional vs. full-likelihood method
div.p: In the second experiment we compare the performances of the fulllikelihood approach against the conditional one. A clever idea is to begin with a conditional estimation (that is faster), and then to perform a full-likelihood search around the values found in the first step. We expect the estimated parameters and the likelihood value to improve after the second estimation, while the estimation time will certainly increase.
To do that, we repeatedly generated (1000 times) two DGPs, one for SAR probit and one for SEM probit, with the following set of parameters: n=1000, ρ and λ in {0, 0.2, 0.4, 0.8}, nn=4 and o W =6.

The results show that the value of the log-likelihood of the second estimation is always slightly lower than the one of the first estimation (between 0.1% and 1% improvement, statistically significant at 5% confidence level). The comparison of the estimation times, instead, is totally in favour of the conditional estimation, as show in Table 2. With respect to the value of the estimated parameters, we found no clear advantage of the full-likelihood approach w.r.t. the conditional one. We expected the second method to be more accurate than the first, but it is not always the case: sometimes the differences are not statistically significant, sometimes they favour the conditional estimation, others the full-likelihood one. The explanation lies in the fact that both the conditional and full-likelihood approach are based on an approximation of the true likelihood, and hence the relative small improvement in terms of log-likelihood achieved by the full-likelihood approach is not sufficient to correct the bias of the estimated parameter, since it is masked by the bigger approximation error. In general, we can conclude that the conditional estimator is capable of reaching a reasonable neighbourhood of the minimum of the true likelihood function. A fulllikelihood approach can later be attempted, but its result is not guaranteed to be better, while it will be surely more time-consuming.

div.head: Experiment 3: Conditional-likelihood estimations for big sample sizes
div.p: The last experiment is intended to test the performance of the proposed conditional-likelihood method w.r.t. sample size. To do that, we repeatedly generated (1000 times) two DGPs, one for SAR probit and one for SEM probit, with the following set of parameters: n ∈ {10 000, 100 000, 1 000 000}, nn ∈ {2, 4, 10} for n = 10 000, nn ∈ {2, 4} for n = 100 000 and nn=2 for n = 1 000 000, ρ and λ in { -0.8, -0.4, -0.2, 0, 0.2, 0.4, 0.8} and o W =6. On each generated data-set we tested the conditional-likelihood method, both with the variance-covariance matrix (UC) and with the precision matrix (UP), and a standard probit (SP) for benchmarking. For each simulation we recorded the obtained parameters and the estimation time. In the following Tables 3, 4 and 5 we summarise the results of the Monte Carlo experiment for the three sizes n ∈ {10 000, 100 000, 1 000 000}. In each table, for each nn and ρ, we report the mean value, standard deviation and RMSE of the estimated parameters β β ρ ( , , ) 0 1 and
. Table 6 reports the mean estimation time of the experiments.

The results obtained in these experiments confirm the good performance of the conditional likelihood estimator, both in terms of accuracy than in terms of estimation time. As expected, we observe that the parameters β β ρ λ ( , , , ) 0 1 are better estimated for the method using the variance-covariance matrix (UC), instead of the precision matrix (UP). This comes at a cost: the UC method is always slower than the UP one, with time differences increasing as the number of neighbours increase (see Table 6). In general, we found that both SAR and SEM probit estimators have a tendency to underestimate the spatial dependence parameter, especially when the true value is very high ρ λ ( , = 0.8) or very low ρ λ ( , = -0.8), and this produce a bias also in the regression parameters β 0 and β 1 . Nevertheless, this effects seems to be mitigated by considering a higher number of neighbours nn.

If we look at the performance of the Standard Probit (SP) model, we can observe that it has a moderate to strong bias in the estimation of the β 1 parameter, especially when the spatial dependence parameter (either ρ or λ) is very high or very low.

To conclude, we would like to stress the impressive reduction in computation time that we have been able to achieve: in Calabrese and Elkink (2014), the Recursive Importance Sampling method (RIS) by Beron and Vijverberg (2004) and the Gibbs Sampling method by LeSage (2000) were the only algorithms performing reasonably well in terms of accuracy for n=1500, but always at a pace of around 10 000 seconds, with peaks of 14.5 hours for certain simulations. The comparison with our proposal is astounding: on a similar data set (n=1000, nn=4), we performed in around one second, more than a ten-thousandth of their time. This allowed us to run the algorithms on simulated datasets with as much as 1 million observations in less than 10 minutes with a contiguity matrix W, something never achieved before for spatial discrete choice models.

div.head: Empirical application
div.p: In this section we test the performance of the proposed algorithm for SAR probit estimation on a urban-sprawl dataset, based on parcel data of 26 municipalities in the Southern France region of Provence. The data analyzed in this application represent just a small sample of a complete survey of all parcels in the region, gathered in the context of the Urbansimul project. 6 The database contains information on the physical characteristics of more than sixty thousands parcels, such as slope, flat surface, altitude and distance to services and amenities, plus other variables on the municipality, notably municipal population (see Table 7 for the descriptive statistics). Out of 60 826 parcels, we know that 19 733 of them were already developed in 1980 (32.44%), while the remaining 41 093 were non-developed (67.56%). In 2008, twentyeight years later, 29 536 parcels out of the 41 093 undeveloped parcels remained undeveloped (71.87%), while 11 557 become developed (28.13%). Finally, in 2015, 614 more parcels become developed.

A spatial probit model is applied to the 41093 undeveloped parcels in 1980 in order to predict which of them have become developed in 2008. In order to take into account those parcels that were already developed in 1980, and that will surely have an influence on the probability of construction in 2008 (urban sprawl around existing urban areas), we added the smoothed variable My 1980 to the set of covariates, where the spatial weight matrix M (60 826 × 41 093) is computed using the first 50 neighbors and y 1980 (of length 60 826) represents developed (1) and undeveloped (0) parcels at 1980. We also benchmarked the SAR probit against a non-spatial probit model, over the same set of covariates. To improve the quality of the estimation, we first fit a Multivariate Adaptive Regression Splines (MARS) model with probit link function. MARS is a non-parametric regression technique that extends the linear model in order to automatically account for nonlinearities. For ease of interpretation, we forced MARS to fit piecewise linear regression using the library earth of R (Milborrow, 2011). After choosing the set of best cuts for piecewise linear regression (cuts are reported in the last column of Table 7), the model further selects the most significative variables.

The spatial weight matrix W of the SAR probit model has been constructed using the 20 first nearest neighbours: we also explored other options and 20 neighbours resulted to be the best choice. In light of the results of the Monte Carlo experiments and the features of the problem (41 093 observations and W with 20 nearest neighbours), we chose to perform the SAR probit estimation via the CLUP estimator (Conditional log-likelihood with precision matrix) and an order of approximation of I ρW ( -) n -1 equal to six. The complete SAR estimation took less than 5 minutes (283 secs.) on a regular desk computer. The estimated coefficients for the two models are reported in Table 8 (all coefficients are significant at 5% confidence level for both models). The results shows that the coefficients of the non-spatial model have the same sign than the coefficients of SAR probit model, with generally higher absolute values (except for the coefficients of slope) and that they are at least two standard deviations away from the spatial estimates. This is consistent with significant bias in the non-spatial estimates. In terms of interpretation of the regression coefficients, we know that the effect of the variation of one regressor on the dependent variable (for both the standard and the spatial probit) is non linear and the link is determined by the standard normal density. Furthermore, for spatial models that involves spatial lags of the output variable (such as our SAR probit), changes in the value of one covariate for one Table 3 Mean, s.d. and RMSE of β β ρ λ ( , , , ) 0 1

Hence, we can distinguish between the impact that a change in one variable at one location has on the expected probability at that same location (direct effect) and on the surrounding observations (indirect effects). The sum of direct and indirect marginal effects is called total marginal effect. 7We report in Table 8 the marginal effects of the standard and spatial probit, and for the latter we distinguish between direct, indirect and total average effects. We observe that total effects of the SAR model are similar to the marginal effects of the non-spatial one, while it seems that indirect effects are always around twice the direct effects for the spatial model. Nevertheless, we recall that indirect effects are cumulated over all neighbours of an observation, hence the individual indirect impact of a single parcel is likely to be smaller then the direct effect. These results illustrates even further the importance of including spatial spillovers in the model.

The direct interpretation of the marginal effects of the two models are complicated by the use of piecewise linear regression. Nevertheless, we can grasp the type of change of the conditional probability of the outcome variable according to the change of the regressors by looking at Fig. 2. There, we can easily appreciate some typical effects of variables such as the distance to the road (for the first 250 meters, the effect on the probability of construction is positive, the more distant the better, due to noise avoidance, while it becomes negative after that threshold, since proximity to the road is considered as an asset) or the distance to the city center (within the borders of the city centre and in the following 50 meters, the effect on the probability of new constructions is positive, due to the scarcity of free parcels and it becomes negative after that threshold). Other topographical (slope, altitude, exposition and flat surface) and demographical (population at 1968 and 1982) variables are harder to interpret, since they contribute simultaneously to the probability of new constructions. Finally, we wanted to assess the ability of the estimated SAR probit model to predict the likelihood of a parcel to become developed in 2015: amongst the 29 536 undeveloped parcels in 2008, 27 010 were correctly predicted as undeveloped by the SAR probit model (true negatives), while the remaining 2526 parcels were predicted as developed (false positive). We observe that, out of the 614 new developed parcels in 2015, 396 of them belong to the set of true negatives, while the remaining 218 to set of false positive. This means that the probability of becoming developed in 2015, is 5.8 times higher on a 2008-false-positive parcel than on a 2008-true-negative one (218/ 2526=8.56% vs. 396/27010=1.46%), suggesting that our model is able to foresee market signals with a certain accuracy.

div.head: Conclusions
div.p: In this paper we studied spatial autoregressive and spatial error models with binary-dependent variables. These models are of particular interest in several disciplines, in particular those that deal with dependent variables that represent some kind of choice, decision or action (between only two possible alternatives) and where the observations are spatially correlated. The concept of spatial interdependence, whether it comes from a direct geographical proximity of the observations of any other sort of contiguity measure (think for example to the relationships between members of a social network), is of major concern for the analysts and ignoring it can generate inefficient and inconsistent estimates (McMillen, 1992).

The approximation is obtained by means of an improved version of the univariate conditioning procedure for MVN probabilities proposed by Mendell and Elston (1974). Two of our estimators (FLUC and FLUP) maximise directly the full log-likelihood function (with computed analytical gradients), while the other two (CLUC and CLUP) use a conditional approach in which intermediate estimations of the covariates parameters, conditional to the value of the spatial parameter, are used to improve the value of the log-likelihood. Moreover, the methods FLUC and CLUC operate directly on the variance-covariance matrix of the likelihood function, while the FLUP and CLUP operate on its inverse, the precision matrix, since it is usually sparser and hence leads to faster computations.

The proposed methods are tested by means of a simulation study in order to assess their performance in terms of accuracy and computation time. The results show that the full-likelihood estimators FLUC and FLUP are not outperforming their conditional counterparts CLUC and CLUP, that indeed prove to be very efficient and reliable. In fact, they recover accurately the value of the true parameters, with only some bias for the spatial dependence parameter, when the true absolute value is high. This effect can be caused by the error due to the approximation used for the computation of the likelihood function, that masks the small differences between the minima found by the conditional and the full-likelihood approaches. A very interesting property of the conditional methods CLUC and CLUP is that they do not suffer from the contagion effect caused by a bad estimation of the spatial dependence parameter, a frequent and troubling issue observed for other methods, as testified in a recent review by Calabrese and Elkink (2014). Furthermore, the speed of the conditional methods is remarkably higher than any other proposal found in the literature: we can easily reduce the estimation time by several orders of magnitude, with no detriment of results accuracy. This allowed us to fit SAR and SEM probit models on synthetic datasets containing as much as 1 million observations in less than 10 minutes and on a urban-sprawl study with more than 40 thousands observations in less than 5 minutes.

In the light of the good performances obtained with the proposed estimators, we will further investigate the possibility to apply the same methodology for the estimation of a SARAR(1,1) probit model, where both spatial autocorrelation and spatial error dependence are present. Moreover, the possibility of rapidly estimating several spatial binary choice models will allow to study spatial nested choice models with more than two alternatives. For us, the next goal is to estimate multinomial spatial probit model, as already attempted by in Bhat (2011).
All the functions used in this paper have been made available in the R package ProbitSpatial on the Comprehensive R Archive Network website. 8

div.p: Appendix C. On the order of the Taylor approximation
In order to establish a good choice for the value of the parameter o W , i.e. the order of the Taylor approximation of I ρW ( -

, we repeatedly generated (1000 times) a SAR probit DGP, with the following set of parameters: n=1000, ρ ∈ {0.2, 0.4, 0.8}, nn ∈ {2, 4, 6, 10} and o W in {1, 2, …, 10}. For each simulation, we recorded the value of the estimated values β β ρ (

and the estimation time. Fig. 3 shows the distribution of the bias of the estimated ρ parameter w.r.t. the value of o W (the bias of β β ( , ) 0 1 showed a stable behaviour and is not represented here). The observation of the graphics confirms that a suitable choice for the order of approximation is around 5 or 6: values smaller than 4 can lead to biased estimations, while higher values do not guarantee better performances and are hence unnecessarily more time-consuming. Furthermore, we observe that the estimation time for a single repetition always amounts to less than 30 seconds, a very good performance compared to the sample size. Such reduced estimation time allows the practitioner interested in finding the best value of o W for a given dataset, to implement his own Monte Carlo experience: from a new set of observations, he can estimate a first Standard Probit model in order to obtain a vector of β . After that, he repeatedly simulate a SAR probit DGP with the spatial weight matrix W, i.e. y β X ϵ I ρW = ( + )( -), n where ρ can be chosen arbitrary and ϵ σ I 0 ∼ ( , ) n 2 . With the generated samples, a SAR probit estimation can be conducted for different values of o W , in order to assess a good choice of the order of approximation. We recommend the practitioner to choose a reasonable dimension for the sample size (e.g. 1000 observations) and a good coverage of the coordinates space.

note.p: We use the golden-section search optimization function optimize for the optimization task, and glm for the Standard Probit. Both functions belongs to the stats library in R (R Core Team, 2013).

A similar experiment has been performed under a different error specification, ceteris paribus. The results confirm the robustness of our SAR and SEM probit estimators, in fact we obtain similar performances in terms of bias of the estimated parameters even under the t-Student distribution of the error term. Furthermore, we find that the SAR and SEM models are always outperforming the corresponding standard probit estimations, independently of the error specification.
The R code is available in the supplementary material ofCalabrese and Elkink (2014).

The full-likelihood optimisation has been performed by means of the optim function of the stats library in R. We adopted the Broyden-Fletcher-Goldfarb-Shanno (BFGS) algorithm, that is a quasi-Newton iterative method for solving unconstrained nonlinear optimization problems. It uses function and gradient values to build up a picture of the surface to be optimized. The analytic expressions of the gradients are provided in Appendix B.
For more details on the computation of marginal effects of spatial probit models, seeLeSage and Pace (2008) andLeSage et al. (2011).
